proof:
The ordinary centroid of $M$ belongs to $M$. By fact 6769574fc1bd9f8d with the full mass $m$, its centroid cap in direction $u$ has volume at least $\Gamma m$. Use the scalar complementary-cap lemma in f0399a8f0bae48c6 with endpoint volumes both $a$, middle body exactly $M$, $f(x)=u\cdot x$, $\tau=u\cdot g_M$, and opposite threshold shifts $\pm t$. The residual volume in $M$ is at most $(1-\Gamma)m$. Its lower bound on captured endpoint mass is nonincreasing in that residual. Dividing by $a$ gives
$$
 P/a\ge[1-(2[(1-\Gamma)r]^{1/d}-1)_+^d]_+ .
$$

The binomial theorem gives $(1+1/d)^d\ge2$ and the logarithm inequality $\log(1+x)<x$ for $x>0$ gives $(1+1/d)^d<e$. The exponential series through degree three and a geometric bound on the subsequent terms give $e<8/3+(1/24)/(1-1/5)=87/32<11/4$. Hence $4/11<\Gamma\le1/2$. Put $x=[(1-\Gamma)r]^{1/d}$. Since $1/2\le(1-\Gamma)r<7/8$, we have $1/2\le x<1$ and $0\le2x-1\le x^2$. The preceding residual bound is therefore at least $1-x^{2d}=1-(1-\Gamma)^2r^2$.

The difference between this last bound and $\Gamma(2-r)$ is concave in $r$. Its values at $1$ and $11/8$ are $\Gamma(1-\Gamma)$ and $\delta_d$. The difference $64[\delta_d-\Gamma(1-\Gamma)]=-57+138\Gamma-57\Gamma^2$ is increasing on $[4/11,1/2]$ and is $-9/4$ at the right endpoint, so the smaller endpoint in $r$ is $11/8$. The concave polynomial $64\delta_d$ takes values $55/121$ and $55/4$ at $\Gamma=4/11$ and $\Gamma=1/2$, proving the positive lower bound. It is increasing on that interval, so $\delta_d\le55/256$ and $c_d<2$.

In the lifted hull, any representation of a point at base zero uses equal weights on the two endpoints. Grouping each fiber's summands by convexity, its continuous coordinate is a mixture of a point in $K$ and a point in $M$. Thus the middle fiber is exactly $K$. The extreme bases give exactly $A,B$ and there are no other integer bases. The total mixed volume is $k+2a$. Any containing halfspace includes its parallel halfspace through the selected point. Through $(0,g_M)$ a nonzero continuous normal gives exactly the two shifts used above and an own cap in $K$ containing the corresponding centroid cap in $M$. The raw mass is at least $\Gamma m+P\ge c_da$. For a purely integer normal the closed cap contains all of $K$ and one whole endpoint. Its mass is $k+a\ge2a>c_da$. Through $(0,g_K)$ the full-mass centroid bound on $K$ alone gives at least $\Gamma k$ in every continuous direction, and a purely integer normal includes all of $K$.

The first guaranteed fraction $c_da/(k+2a)$ decreases in $k/a$ and the second $\Gamma k/(k+2a)$ increases. They agree at $k/a=c_d/\Gamma$, where the common value is $\Gamma c_d/(c_d+2\Gamma)$. The choice in the statement takes their maximum, whose minimum is that value. Since $c_d>2\Gamma$, it is strictly greater than $\Gamma/2$.

statement:
Let $d\ge1$ and let $A,K,B$ be $d$-dimensional convex bodies with $|A|=|B|=a>0$ and $M=(A+B)/2\subseteq K$. Write $m=|M|$, $k=|K|$, $r=m/a$, $\Gamma=(d/(d+1))^d$ and let $g_M,g_K$ denote their ordinary centroids. Suppose $1\le r\le11/8$. Set
$$
 \delta_d=\frac{-57+202\Gamma-121\Gamma^2}{64}\ge\frac{55}{7744}>0,
 \qquad c_d=2\Gamma+\delta_d.
$$
For every $u\ne0$ and real $t$, let $P$ be the sum of the $A$ and $B$ cap volumes for the inequalities $u\cdot x\ge u\cdot g_M+t$ and $u\cdot x\ge u\cdot g_M-t$, respectively. Then
$$
 P/a\ge 1-(1-\Gamma)^2r^2\ge\Gamma(2-r)+\delta_d.
$$

Place $A,K,B$ at bases $-1,0,1$ in their lifted convex hull, and measure the resulting three integer fibers by the sum of their ordinary volumes. At $(0,g_M)$ and $(0,g_K)$ the raw depths are at least $c_da$ and $\Gamma k$, respectively. Choose $(0,g_M)$ if $k/a\le c_d/\Gamma$, and $(0,g_K)$ otherwise. The selected point has normalized depth at least $\Gamma c_d/(c_d+2\Gamma)>\Gamma/2$ over all closed ambient halfspaces containing it.
title: A Minkowski-volume surplus window for two specified middle centroids
